set.detail: Theodosius I died of dropsy at Milan on 17 January 395, four months after the Frigidus, with both his sons already Augusti. Arcadius, about seventeen, was in Constantinople under the praetorian prefect Rufinus; Honorius, ten, was with his father in Milan, and the magister militum Stilicho, married to Theodosius's niece and adopted daughter Serena, claimed that the dying emperor had entrusted both boys to his care. Ambrose's funeral oration of 25 February and Claudian's later poems are the voices of that claim. Nothing in law divided the empire. Laws continued to be issued in the names of both emperors, each half recognised the other's consul, and the Theodosian Code of 438 applied everywhere. But practice diverged at once. The eastern field army that had won the Frigidus was in Italy; Stilicho sent it home under Gainas, whose men cut down Rufinus at the Hebdomon parade ground on 27 November 395 in front of Arcadius. The quarrel over the prefecture of Illyricum, whose eastern dioceses of Dacia and Macedonia had been attached to Constantinople in 379, poisoned relations for a decade: the eastern court declared Stilicho a public enemy in 397, and Stilicho's plan to annex eastern Illyricum with Alaric's help in 407-408 helped bring him down. The consequences were structural. The East had the richer and more defensible tax base of Egypt, Syria and Anatolia, a single capital behind the sea and later the Theodosian Walls, and a single long frontier with an often peaceful Persia. The West had the longer Rhine and Danube frontier, the weaker fiscal system and the more powerful landed aristocracy. Historians therefore treat 395 as the conventional date of the partition, while stressing that contemporaries saw one empire under two emperors, and that the courts' mutual suspicion, rather than any constitutional act, made the split permanent. Eastern help to the West continued sporadically until 468.
set.debate: Whether Theodosius really named Stilicho guardian of both sons rests on Stilicho's own propaganda (Claudian, Ambrose); eastern sources ignore it.

scholarship: Cameron and Long, Barbarians and Politics at the Court of Arcadius (1993)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
McEvoy, Child Emperor Rule in the Late Roman West (2013)

set.detail: Alaric was a Gothic noble who had commanded federates in Theodosius's army at the Frigidus in 394, where the Goths bore the brunt of the fighting and, Orosius said, their losses were a double victory for Rome. Disappointed of a Roman command and probably of the pay and supplies due to his men, he rose in 395 at the head of a mixed force of Goths and others settled in Thrace and Moesia since the treaty of 382. They ravaged Thrace and Macedonia and appeared before Constantinople, where Rufinus negotiated in person, perhaps dressed in Gothic clothes as his enemies claimed. Alaric then moved through Thessaly, where Stilicho, leading both eastern and western armies, faced him but was ordered by Arcadius to send the eastern troops home. With the pass of Thermopylae apparently left open, the Goths swept into Greece in 396. Athens paid to be spared, while Corinth, Argos and Sparta were sacked; Eunapius, a pagan, blamed Christian monks for leading the Goths through Thermopylae and claimed the sanctuary of Eleusis was destroyed. In 397 Stilicho landed in the Peloponnese and trapped Alaric at Pholoe in Arcadia, but the Goths escaped across the Gulf of Corinth into Epirus. Constantinople then made Alaric magister militum per Illyricum, giving him legal access to the arsenals and supplies of the region: a reward for rebellion that Claudian denounced. The episode set the pattern of the next fifteen years. Alaric sought not to destroy the empire but a recognised command, regular pay and land for his people, and played the two courts against each other. Modern scholarship debates whether his following was already an ethnic 'Visigothic' people or a Roman army of mixed origin formed in imperial service; the term Visigoths is anachronistic for this date.
set.debate: Whether Stilicho deliberately let Alaric escape at Pholoe, and how far Alaric's followers formed a pre-existing people, are both debated.

scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)

set.detail: Alaric invaded Italy in late 401, crossing the Julian Alps while Stilicho was fighting Vandals and Alans in Raetia. The Goths besieged Milan, where Honorius was residing, and the panic led to the court's move to Ravenna in 402. Stilicho returned with troops withdrawn from the Rhine and Britain, relieved Milan and followed the Goths west into Liguria. On Easter Sunday, 6 April 402, near Pollentia (Pollenzo, south of Turin), his army, led in the first attack by the Alan commander Saul, assaulted Alaric's camp, apparently counting on the Arian Goths' unwillingness to fight on the feast. Orosius, writing a decade later, condemns Saul for violating Easter and claims the pagan general was punished when the Alans were at first repulsed and Saul killed. The battle was hard-fought and inconclusive in the field, but the Romans captured the Gothic camp with its plunder and Alaric's wife and children. Claudian's De bello Gothico, recited in Rome in 402, presents it as a triumph to rank with the defeat of the Cimbri, while the Christian chroniclers are more guarded. Alaric withdrew, negotiated and then tried to break into Raetia; in summer 402, or perhaps 403, Stilicho defeated him again at Verona, where Alaric nearly lost his life, and the Goths retreated to Illyricum. The significance of Pollentia lay less in the fighting than in the strategic choices: Stilicho preferred to keep Alaric's army intact as a potential ally for his ambitions in eastern Illyricum rather than destroy it, a choice his enemies later portrayed as treason. The withdrawal of garrisons to defend Italy also weakened the Rhine frontier four years before the crossing of 406.
set.debate: The date of Verona (402 or 403) and whether Pollentia was a Roman victory at all are disputed; Jordanes makes it a Gothic one.

scholarship: Cameron, Claudian (1970)
Hughes, Stilicho (2010)

set.detail: In late 405 a pagan Gothic king, Radagaisus, crossed the Alps from the middle Danube with a large following that Zosimus inflates to 400,000 and Orosius to 200,000; modern estimates of perhaps 20,000 warriors with families are more plausible. The invasion probably reflected pressure from the Huns on the peoples of the Hungarian plain. Radagaisus split his force and with the main body advanced deep into Italy, besieging Florence in summer 406. Stilicho gathered thirty numeri, the core of the Italian field army, together with Hunnic auxiliaries under Uldin and Goths under Sarus, and relieved the city. The invaders retreated onto the heights of Faesulae, where Stilicho surrounded them with field works and starved them out rather than fight a pitched battle. Radagaisus tried to escape, was captured and executed on 23 August 406. Orosius, delighting in a pagan's defeat in answer to pagan claims that Rome suffered for abandoning the gods, says the captives were so numerous that they were sold for a solidus a head and died so quickly that their buyers lost their money. Some 12,000 of the best warriors were enrolled in the Roman army, where they became a powerful element among Stilicho's federates. The victory was celebrated with an arch in Rome. Its consequences were mixed. It confirmed Stilicho's prestige, but the troops gathered for Italy were not available on the Rhine when the Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed at the end of 406, and the 12,000 federates of Radagaisus later deserted to Alaric after Stilicho's fall, swelling his army at the decisive moment.
set.debate: Numbers are wildly inflated in the sources; the date is fixed by the Fasti Vindobonenses (23 August 406) for Radagaisus's execution.

scholarship: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007)

set.detail: Prosper's chronicle places the crossing on 31 December 406: Hasding and Siling Vandals, Alans and Suebi, groups that had been moving west from the middle Danube under Hunnic pressure, entered Gaul near Mainz. Gregory of Tours, quoting the lost history of Renatus Profuturus Frigeridus, records a preliminary battle in which Frankish federates killed the Vandal king Godegisel and some 20,000 of his men until the Alans under Respendial came to the rescue. The image of a frozen Rhine comes from later embellishment and is not in the sources. Michael Kulikowski has argued that the crossing should be dated to 405, with Prosper's year a scribal confusion, a view that has won some support. Once across, the invaders spread through Belgica and northern Gaul. Jerome, writing from Bethlehem in 409, lists the cities ravaged: Mainz destroyed and thousands massacred in its church, Worms, Reims, Amiens, Arras, Tournai, Speyer and Strasbourg taken, Aquitaine and Narbonensis devastated, with only Toulouse holding out thanks to its bishop. The Gallic poems On Providence and the Commonitorium of Orientius convey the sense of catastrophe. The crossing had immediate political consequences. The British army, fearing invasion, raised a series of usurpers culminating in Constantine III, who crossed to Gaul in 407, and the Rhine frontier was never fully restored. After two and a half years in Gaul, the invaders crossed the Pyrenees in 409 and divided Spain among themselves in 411. The Vandals passed on to Africa in 429. In modern historiography the crossing is the single most important event in the transformation of the western provinces, although historians disagree whether it was a desperate flight from the Huns or an opportunistic exploitation of Roman civil strife.
set.debate: Date (31 December 405 or 406) and whether the Rhine was frozen are disputed; the frozen river is a modern myth.

scholarship: Kulikowski, 'Barbarians in Gaul, usurpers in Britain', Britannia 31 (2000)
Heather, Empires and Barbarians (2009)
Goffart, Barbarian Tides (2006)

set.detail: The crossing of the Rhine and the probable withdrawal of units to defend Italy left the British garrison feeling abandoned. In 406 it proclaimed a soldier named Marcus, then killed him and chose a civilian official, Gratian, who lasted four months; in early 407 it raised a common soldier, Flavius Claudius Constantinus, chosen, Orosius says, only for the auspicious name. Constantine crossed to Boulogne with the British field army, won over the remaining troops in Gaul, fought or bought off the Rhine invaders and secured the Rhine frontier with treaties with the Franks, Alamanni and Burgundians. Stilicho sent the Goth Sarus, who defeated and killed Constantine's general Justinian and besieged Valence, but was driven back over the Alps by Constantine's commanders Gerontius and Edobichus. Constantine made Arles his capital and sent his son Constans, a former monk raised to Caesar, with Gerontius to take Spain from the relatives of Theodosius who held it for Honorius; two of them, Didymus and Verinianus, were captured and executed, while their kinsmen raised peasant levies in the Pyrenees. In 409 the hard-pressed Honorius, threatened by Alaric, recognised Constantine as co-emperor and sent him a purple robe; Constantine promised help against Alaric and may have marched into Italy in 410 before retreating. His empire then fell apart. Gerontius rebelled in Spain in 409 with his own emperor Maximus, apparently admitting the Vandals, Alans and Suebi into the peninsula, and killed Constans at Vienne. Constantine was besieged at Arles first by Gerontius and then by Honorius's new general Constantius; he surrendered in 411, was ordained a priest and murdered with his son Julian on the way to Ravenna. His usurpation is the last act of Roman Britain's military history: the army he took to Gaul never returned.

scholarship: Drinkwater, 'The usurpers Constantine III and Jovinus', Britannia 29 (1998)
Kulikowski, 'Barbarians in Gaul, usurpers in Britain', Britannia 31 (2000)

set.detail: By 408 Stilicho was vulnerable. The Rhine had been breached, Constantine III held Gaul, Alaric was in Noricum demanding 4,000 lb of gold for his services in the abortive Illyrian campaign, and Stilicho had forced a reluctant Senate to pay, provoking the senator Lampadius's remark that 'this is not peace but a pact of servitude'. When Arcadius died in May 408, Stilicho proposed to go to Constantinople himself to secure the child Theodosius II, and dissuaded Honorius from going. The court official Olympius, a magister scrinii from the Black Sea, spread the rumour that Stilicho intended to put his own son Eucherius on the eastern throne. On 13 August 408, at Ticinum, where Honorius was reviewing troops gathered for Gaul, the soldiers mutinied and murdered the praetorian prefects of Italy and Gaul, the magister officiorum, the quaestor and other Stilicho loyalists. Stilicho, at Bononia with his barbarian federates, refused their offer to attack the Roman troops and went to Ravenna, where he took sanctuary in a church. Lured out by an oath that he would only be detained, he was then shown a second order for his execution and, Zosimus says, forbade his retainers to resist and offered his neck to the sword of Heraclianus on 22 August 408. Eucherius was hunted down in Rome and killed; Honorius divorced Stilicho's daughter Thermantia; Serena was strangled in Rome later that year on suspicion of collusion with Alaric. The most serious consequence followed at once: Roman troops in Italian cities massacred the wives and children of barbarian federates, and some 30,000 soldiers, Zosimus says, went over to Alaric, who now invaded Italy unopposed. Modern historians see the coup as the triumph of an anti-barbarian court faction, but also as a reaction to Stilicho's policy of placating Alaric while Gaul was lost.
set.debate: Whether Stilicho really planned to place Eucherius on a throne cannot be proven; Orosius and Rutilius believed it, Zosimus (from Olympiodorus) did not.

scholarship: Hughes, Stilicho (2010)
Matthews, Western Aristocracies and Imperial Court (1975)

set.detail: After Stilicho's execution, Alaric, reinforced by the deserting federates, offered peace for a modest sum and an exchange of hostages; Olympius's government refused. In autumn 408 the Goths marched down the Via Flaminia, bypassing Ravenna, and blockaded Rome, seizing Portus and cutting off the Tiber supply from the grain depots. Famine and plague followed; Zosimus describes corpses lying in the streets and rumours of cannibalism, and says that the pagan Etruscan diviners offered to call down lightning on the besiegers with the approval of Pope Innocent, provided the rites were performed privately, which the Senate refused. Serena, Stilicho's widow, was strangled on the Senate's orders on suspicion of plotting to admit the Goths. Finally the Senate sent envoys, among them Basilius and the tribune John, who were told by Alaric that 'thicker hay is easier to mow' when they warned of the city's numbers. He demanded all the gold and silver in the city and all slaves of barbarian origin, and when asked what he would leave answered 'your lives'. The settlement eventually agreed was 5,000 lb of gold, 30,000 lb of silver, 4,000 silk tunics, 3,000 scarlet-dyed skins and 3,000 lb of pepper. To raise it, statues of the gods were melted down, among them, the pagan Zosimus noted, an image of Virtue, after which Roman courage vanished. Some 40,000 slaves fled to the Goths. Alaric withdrew to Etruria and opened talks with Ravenna for land in Noricum and a high command. The first siege showed that Rome, defended by the Aurelian Walls and a large but unarmed population, could be starved into submission without an assault, and it set the stage for the second siege of 409 and the sack of 410.

scholarship: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Lipps, Machado and von Rummel (eds.), The Sack of Rome in 410 AD (2013)

set.detail: Hydatius, a bishop in Gallaecia and the main narrator of these events, dates the crossing of the Pyrenees to 28 September or 12 October 409, the day varying in the manuscripts. The invaders who had crossed the Rhine in 406, the Hasding and Siling Vandals, Alans and Suebi, passed through the mountains apparently with the connivance of Gerontius, Constantine III's general in Spain, who had just rebelled and proclaimed Maximus. Orosius accuses the Honoriaci, barbarian units who had replaced the local Spanish guards of the passes, of letting them through. For two years, Hydatius says, they ravaged the peninsula while famine drove men to cannibalism, plague followed, and wild beasts fed on the dead, the four plagues of the Apocalypse. In 411, apparently by treaty with Maximus's regime, the invaders divided the provinces by lot: the Hasdings and Suebi took Gallaecia, the Alans Lusitania and Carthaginiensis, and the Silings Baetica, while the Romans retained Tarraconensis. The settlement turned Spain into a patchwork. Honorius's government responded by using the Goths: from 416 Wallia, acting as a Roman federate, destroyed the Silings and so mauled the Alans that their survivors placed themselves under the Hasding king. The Hasdings, now leading a Vandal-Alan confederation, moved to Baetica in 419-420, defeated the Roman general Castinus in 422 and took to the sea, raiding the Balearics and Mauretania before crossing to Africa in 429. The Suebi remained in Gallaecia and built a kingdom that lasted until 585. Archaeologically the invasion is hard to trace, and many historians now emphasise that most Hispano-Roman towns continued to function, with local elites negotiating with the newcomers.
set.debate: The precise date and Gerontius's role are uncertain; the allotment of 411 may have been a formal treaty with the usurper Maximus.

scholarship: Kulikowski, Late Roman Spain and Its Cities (2004)
Arce, Bárbaros y romanos en Hispania (2005)

set.detail: After two blockades in 408 and 409, and the brief elevation of the senator Priscus Attalus as his puppet emperor, Alaric was negotiating with Honorius near Ravenna in summer 410 when he was attacked by the Goth Sarus, a personal enemy in Roman service. Taking this as proof of bad faith, he marched on Rome. On the night of 24 August 410 the Goths entered by the Salarian Gate, according to Procopius through treachery: either slaves opened it or the noblewoman Proba, pitying the starving people, ordered it opened. The sack lasted three days. Alaric, an Arian Christian, ordered the churches of Peter and Paul respected as sanctuaries, and Orosius tells of a Goth who found a consecrated virgin guarding the sacred vessels of St Peter and escorted her and them in procession to the basilica. But the city was plundered, the Gardens of Sallust burned, houses of the aristocracy on the Aventine and Caelian looted, and many were killed or carried off, among them Honorius's sister Galla Placidia. Wealthy refugees fled to Sicily, Africa and the Holy Land, where Jerome wrote 'the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken'. The physical damage was limited compared with the psychological shock. Pagans blamed the abandonment of the old gods, and Augustine began the City of God in 413 to answer them, arguing that no earthly city was eternal. Orosius minimised the event as less destructive than the fire of Nero. Archaeology confirms burning in the Basilica Aemilia, where coins melted into the floor, and in parts of the Forum. Alaric left after three days, marched south intending to cross to Sicily and Africa, lost his fleet in a storm at the Straits and died near Consentia before the end of 410.

scholarship: Lipps, Machado and von Rummel (eds.), The Sack of Rome in 410 AD (2013)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)

set.detail: Zosimus, drawing on Olympiodorus, says that around 409 the Britons, harried by Saxon raids and abandoned by Constantine III, took up arms, freed their cities from barbarian attack, expelled the Roman officials and set up their own administration, and that the Armoricans followed their example. Elsewhere he says that in 410 Honorius wrote letters to the cities of Britain telling them to look to their own defence. The second passage has been doubted: some scholars, following a suggestion first made in the nineteenth century, argue that Zosimus wrote of Bruttium in southern Italy, which fits the surrounding narrative of Alaric's movements, and that the letter has nothing to do with Britain. Either way, no Roman official is attested in Britain after 409, no field army returned and imported coin ceased to arrive: the latest substantial hoards, such as Hoxne, end with issues of Constantine III and Honorius. The Groans of the Britons, an appeal to Aetius in his third consulship (446), shows that some Britons still thought of Rome as their protector a generation later. Gildas's narrative in the sixth century and Bede's in the eighth are later constructions. Archaeology shows the rapid collapse of the Roman economy in Britain in the early fifth century: towns, villas, coin use and pottery industries disappeared within a generation, a more drastic break than in any other western province. The end of Roman Britain is therefore less a single event than a process, but 409-410 marks the point at which the island ceased to be part of the empire's administration. Its subsequent history, the rule of tyranni such as Vortigern and the settlement of Angles and Saxons, belongs to a different world.
set.debate: Whether Honorius's letter of 410 (Zosimus 6.10.2) was addressed to Britain or Bruttium is disputed.

sources.w: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

scholarship: Esmonde Cleary, The Ending of Roman Britain (1989)
Birley, The Roman Government of Britain (2005)
Halsall, Worlds of Arthur (2013)

set.detail: The land walls that protected Constantinople for a thousand years were built under the regency of Anthemius, praetorian prefect of the East from 405 to 414, during the minority of Theodosius II. A law of 4 April 413 in the Theodosian Code refers to the new wall as complete and assigns the towers to the use of the landowners on whose land they stood. The new line ran some 1.5 km west of Constantine's wall, from the Sea of Marmara near the Golden Gate to the Golden Horn near Blachernae, about 5.7 km long, enclosing much new land for the growing city. The first phase consisted of the great inner wall, about 5 m thick and 12 m high, with 96 towers. After the earthquake of 447 the prefect Constantinus rebuilt the damaged sections in sixty days and added an outer wall with its own towers and a moat some 20 m wide, creating a triple line of defence across the peninsula; inscriptions on the Mevlevihane gate commemorate the feat. The Golden Gate, a triumphal arch of marble, was incorporated into the wall as a ceremonial entrance. The sea walls along the Marmara and the Golden Horn were added and strengthened in the following decades, and in the 620s the Blachernae area was enclosed after the Avar siege. The walls were decisive in the survival of the eastern empire: they withstood the Huns in 447 by deterrence, Vitalian in 515, the Kutrigurs in 559, the Avars and Persians in 626, the Arabs in 674-678 and 717-718, and fell to an assault only in 1204 and 1453. Their construction reflects the confidence and resources of the eastern state in the decade after the sack of Rome.
set.debate: Some scholars think the walls were begun before 405, under Arcadius, and only completed under Anthemius.

scholarship: Van Millingen, Byzantine Constantinople: The Walls of the City (1899)
Meyer-Plath and Schneider, Die Landmauer von Konstantinopel (1943)
Crow, 'The infrastructures of a great city', in Lavan et al., Technology in Transition (2007)

set.detail: After Athaulf's death in 415 and Sigeric's brief reign, the new Gothic king Wallia, starving and blockaded by the Roman fleet, made a treaty with Constantius in 416: in return for 600,000 measures of grain he returned Galla Placidia and fought the Rhine invaders in Spain as a Roman federate. In 416-418 his Goths annihilated the Siling Vandals in Baetica and so mauled the Alans that they joined the Hasdings. In 418 Constantius recalled them and settled them in Aquitania Secunda, with some adjacent cities of Novempopulana and Narbonensis, between Toulouse and the Atlantic. The terms are much debated. Older scholarship, following later Burgundian and Visigothic law codes, assumed the Goths received a share, two-thirds or one-third, of the land of Roman estates under the system of hospitalitas. Walter Goffart argued instead that they were assigned shares of tax revenue, not land; most scholars now see a combination of land grants and tax assignments varying from place to place. Why the Goths were settled in prosperous south-western Gaul, rather than on a frontier, is also disputed: suggested reasons include protecting Aquitaine against Bacaudae and Saxon raiders, keeping the Goths away from the Mediterranean and Italy, and rewarding them near the Atlantic grain lands. In the same year Honorius re-established the council of the Seven Provinces at Arles, giving the Gallo-Roman aristocracy a forum. The settlement was meant to create a dependent federate force. Wallia died in 418 and was succeeded by Theodoric I, under whom the Goths fought both for and against Rome. From this base grew the Visigothic kingdom of Toulouse, which by 475 covered most of Gaul south of the Loire and much of Spain.
set.debate: Land versus tax shares, and the date (418 or 419; Prosper and Hydatius differ), are disputed.

scholarship: Goffart, Barbarians and Romans AD 418-584: The Techniques of Accommodation (1980)
Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007)

set.detail: The Notitia Dignitatum, 'list of offices', survives only in Renaissance copies of a lost Carolingian manuscript from Speyer. It lists every senior civil and military post of the two halves of the empire with their staffs and, for military commanders, the units under them and their stations, with painted illustrations of insignia, shield patterns of the regiments, and personifications of provinces. The eastern section appears to reflect conditions around 395-400 and was not updated. The western section was revised piecemeal into the 420s: it includes units raised by Honorius and Constantius III and reflects the losses of the 410s, but entries for Britain and the Rhine may be fossilised. It was evidently a working document of the primicerius notariorum, who issued letters of appointment, and was probably copied for the western court around 425-430. The Notitia is the fundamental source for the late Roman army. It shows the division into mobile field armies (comitatenses and palatini) under magistri militum and frontier troops (limitanei) under duces and comites, the proliferation of small units, the names of new regiments such as the Honoriani and Theodosiani, and in the West the transfer of frontier units into field armies (pseudocomitatenses). It also lists the arms factories (fabricae), mints, weaving mills and treasuries. Its figures, if all units were at full strength, would give an army of 500,000 to 600,000, but scholars regard many units as under strength or existing only on paper. The British chapters, including the dux Britanniarum and the count of the Saxon Shore with its forts from Brancaster to Portchester, are the main evidence for the last Roman garrison of the island. The date, purpose and reliability of each chapter remain subjects of intensive debate.
set.debate: Whether the western Notitia was systematically updated or only patchily revised is debated.

scholarship: Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964), ch. 17
Kulikowski, 'The Notitia Dignitatum as a historical source', Historia 49 (2000)
Brennan, 'The Notitia Dignitatum', in Les littératures techniques dans l'Antiquité (1996)

set.detail: When Honorius died of dropsy at Ravenna on 15 August 423, the eastern court hesitated to recognise anyone, and a western official, the primicerius notariorum Joannes, was proclaimed at Rome with the backing of the general Castinus. Galla Placidia and her children, Justa Grata Honoria and Valentinian, had fled to Constantinople in 423 after quarrelling with Honorius. Theodosius II decided to restore his cousin's line. Valentinian was named Caesar at Thessalonica in October 424 and betrothed to Theodosius's infant daughter Licinia Eudoxia. In 425 an eastern expedition under Ardabur, his son Aspar and the magister Candidianus invaded Italy; Ardabur was captured at sea and held in Ravenna, but Aspar, guided by a shepherd through the marshes, entered the city, and Joannes was captured, paraded on a donkey in the hippodrome at Aquileia and beheaded. Three days later the young Aetius arrived with a Hunnic army said to be 60,000 strong, too late to help Joannes; he was bought off with the command in Gaul. On 23 October 425 the master of offices Helion invested the six-year-old Valentinian as Augustus in Rome. Galla Placidia governed as regent for twelve years, balancing the generals Felix, Bonifatius and Aetius, whose rivalry brought civil war in 432 and contributed to the loss of Africa. In 437 Valentinian went to Constantinople to marry Licinia Eudoxia, and the eastern court received western Illyricum, perhaps including Sirmium, as the price of its support. His reign of thirty years was the longest of any western emperor of the fifth century, but power lay with Aetius until Valentinian killed him in 454.

scholarship: Oost, Galla Placidia Augusta (1968)
McEvoy, Child Emperor Rule in the Late Roman West (2013)

set.detail: The sack of 410 brought refugees to Africa and renewed pagan arguments that Rome had fallen because it abandoned its gods. Prompted by the tribune Marcellus, Augustine began De Civitate Dei in 413 and worked on it for thirteen years, publishing it in instalments until about 426-427. The first ten books are polemical. Books 1-5 argue that the gods never protected Rome, citing Roman history from Varro, Sallust and Livy: the Gauls took the city, Cannae was lost, and civil wars raged while the old cults flourished. Rome's empire was granted by the true God as a reward for the Romans' love of glory, a lesser virtue. Books 6-10 attack pagan theology, Varro's antiquarianism, and the Neoplatonists, whom Augustine admired but faulted for refusing the Incarnation. Books 11-22 present the positive doctrine of two cities, formed by two loves, love of self to the contempt of God and love of God to the contempt of self, intermingled in this world until the Last Judgement: the heavenly city, a pilgrim on earth, and the earthly city, whose highest good is peace. Augustine traced them from the fall of the angels through Cain and Abel, Babylon and Rome, to the end of time, and concluded with the resurrection and eternal rest. The work refuses to identify the Roman empire with God's purpose, against the triumphalist history of Eusebius and Orosius, Augustine's own pupil. Its definition of a people as a multitude bound by common objects of love, and its claim that a kingdom without justice is a great robbery, deeply influenced medieval political thought. The City of God, written as Vandals approached Hippo, is the most important intellectual response to the crisis of the western empire.

scholarship: Brown, Augustine of Hippo (1967, 2000)
Markus, Saeculum: History and Society in the Theology of St Augustine (1970)
O'Daly, Augustine's City of God: A Reader's Guide (1999)

set.detail: In May 429 Gaiseric, king of the Vandals and Alans since 428, led his people from southern Spain across the Straits of Gibraltar, probably from Iulia Traducta (Tarifa) to Tingitana. Victor of Vita says he ordered a count of the whole people, including old men, children and slaves, and found 80,000; Procopius, using the same figure, says Gaiseric organised them into 80 units of 'thousands' to make his army seem larger. The transport of such numbers across 15 km of sea required ships, possibly provided by the Spanish coastal cities or seized in earlier raids on the Balearics. Procopius tells that Bonifatius, comes Africae and at odds with the court of Galla Placidia, invited the Vandals in as allies; most modern historians regard the story as a later invention, since Bonifatius fought them from the start. The Vandals' motives were probably a search for a secure and rich base away from Gothic and Roman pressure in Spain. Advancing east along the coast, they defeated Bonifatius in 430 and besieged Hippo, where Augustine died. In 432 an eastern army under Aspar arrived and was beaten. The treaty of 435 gave the Vandals parts of Mauretania and Numidia as federates; in 439 Gaiseric seized Carthage. The loss of Africa, the West's richest source of tax revenue, grain and olive oil, was the most damaging single blow to the western empire. Heather calculates that Africa provided a major share of western revenues; without it the government could no longer pay for a large army. Gaiseric's fleet also made the western Mediterranean insecure for decades, culminating in the sack of Rome in 455.
set.debate: The figure of 80,000 is suspiciously round; Bonifatius's invitation is probably legend.

scholarship: Courtois, Les Vandales et l'Afrique (1955)
Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)

set.detail: After defeating Bonifatius, the comes Africae, in the field in 430, Gaiseric besieged him in the walled port of Hippo Regius, the second city of Numidia, from about June 430. The siege lasted fourteen months. Inside the city were refugees from the surrounding countryside and many clergy, among them the bishop Augustine, aged 75, and his biographer Possidius, bishop of Calama, who describes the misery of the province: churches burned, clergy killed or tortured, consecrated virgins scattered, and the survivors hiding in mountains and caves. In the third month of the siege, on 28 August 430, Augustine died of fever after asking for the penitential psalms to be written on the wall facing his bed; Possidius says he left no will because he had no property, but bequeathed his library to the church. The library survived the siege, which is how his enormous oeuvre reached posterity. The Vandals, with little siege equipment and suffering from hunger, raised the siege in July 431. Bonifatius, reinforced by an eastern army under Aspar, then offered battle and was defeated again, after which he was recalled to Italy and the Vandals took Hippo, which was largely abandoned by its inhabitants. Gaiseric made it his first capital in Africa, and the treaty of 435 left him in control of much of Numidia. Archaeology at Hippo has revealed the cathedral complex, the so-called Basilica Pacis, possibly Augustine's church. The siege shows the Vandals' limited capacity in siege warfare at this stage, which made them reliant on treaties and surprise, as at Carthage in 439, rather than assault.

scholarship: Brown, Augustine of Hippo (1967, 2000)
Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)

set.detail: The controversy began in 428 when Nestorius, the new patriarch of Constantinople, a monk from Antioch, objected to the title Theotokos, 'bearer of God', for Mary, preferring Christotokos, and emphasised the distinction of Christ's divine and human natures. Cyril of Alexandria attacked him as dividing Christ into two persons, won the support of Pope Celestine, who condemned Nestorius at a Roman synod in August 430, and sent him twelve anathemas. Theodosius II summoned a general council to Ephesus for Pentecost 431. Cyril arrived with some 50 Egyptian bishops and allies among the Asian bishops led by Memnon of Ephesus, and opened the council on 22 June, before John of Antioch and the Syrian bishops arrived, and despite the protest of the imperial commissioner Candidian. In a single session the 150 or more bishops present deposed Nestorius, who refused to attend, and the city celebrated with a torchlight procession in honour of the Theotokos. When John arrived four days later, his 43 bishops held a rival council and deposed Cyril and Memnon. The papal legates then arrived and joined Cyril. Theodosius at first confirmed both depositions and detained Cyril, Memnon and Nestorius, but under pressure from Cyril's gifts to the court and monastic demonstrations in Constantinople he released Cyril and sent Nestorius back to his monastery near Antioch; he was later exiled to the Great Oasis in Egypt, where he wrote the Book of Heracleides. In 433 Cyril and John reconciled in the Formula of Reunion, which accepted Theotokos and two natures in one person. The council, later counted as the Third Ecumenical, left the Church of the East, which honoured Nestorius's teacher Theodore of Mopsuestia, outside imperial communion.

scholarship: McGuckin, St Cyril of Alexandria: The Christological Controversy (1994)
Wessel, Cyril of Alexandria and the Nestorian Controversy (2004)

set.detail: In March 429 Theodosius II ordered a commission to collect all general imperial constitutions issued since Constantine, arranged by subject under titles and in chronological order within each, as a first stage towards a fuller code combining laws and juristic opinion. The second stage was abandoned; in 435 a new commission of sixteen under the former prefect Antiochus was empowered to edit the texts, removing preambles and redundant words and adapting them to make them clear. The result, the Codex Theodosianus in sixteen books with some 2,500 constitutions, was promulgated in Constantinople on 15 February 438 and took effect on 1 January 439 for both halves of the empire. In the West it was presented to the Senate of Rome on 25 December 438 by the praetorian prefect Anicius Acilius Glabrio Faustus, who had brought it from Constantinople after Valentinian III's wedding; the minutes of that session, the Gesta Senatus, survive with the senators' acclamations, repeated dozens of times. The code replaced all earlier collections of constitutions, including the private Gregorian and Hermogenian codes, and later laws, the Novels, were exchanged between the two courts. Books 1-5 cover public offices and private law, 6-8 the civil service, 9 criminal law, 10-11 finance, 12-15 cities and public works, and 16 religion, with laws on heresy, Jews and pagans. The Code is the fundamental source for the institutions of the fourth and early fifth century. In the West it survived through the Visigothic Breviary of Alaric (506), from which the first five books are mainly known, while in the East it was superseded by Justinian's Code (529-534), which drew on it extensively.

scholarship: Harries and Wood (eds.), The Theodosian Code (1993)
Matthews, Laying Down the Law: A Study of the Theodosian Code (2000)
Sirks, The Theodosian Code: A Study (2007)

set.detail: Under the treaty of 435 the Vandals held parts of Mauretania and Numidia as federates, and Gaiseric's son Huneric was sent to Italy as a hostage. In 439, while Aetius and Litorius were fighting the Goths in Gaul, Gaiseric broke the treaty and on 19 October seized Carthage, the second city of the western empire, apparently by surprise and with little fighting. Prosper says he confiscated the property of the nobles and clergy and subjected the people to slavery; many senators and the bishop Quodvultdeus were put on unseaworthy ships and drifted to Naples. Gaiseric dated his reign from this event. With Carthage came its harbour and fleet, and the Vandals soon raided Sicily (440) and besieged Panormus. In 441 a combined eastern and western expedition assembled in Sicily, but the eastern contingent was recalled when the Huns and Persians attacked the eastern frontier. In 442 Valentinian III made a treaty recognising Vandal possession of Proconsularis, Byzacena and eastern Numidia in exchange for the Mauretanias and western Numidia. Carthage became the Vandal capital and Gaiseric's kingdom the first independent barbarian kingdom on Roman soil, with its own royal dating and coinage. The fiscal consequences for the West were severe: a law of 440 granting tax relief to refugees, and another of 445 reducing the taxes of Numidia and Mauretania to one-eighth, show the loss. Vandal confiscations created a lasting religious conflict between Arian rulers and Catholic subjects, described by Victor of Vita. Control of Carthage gave Gaiseric naval power that made him master of the western Mediterranean for forty years.

scholarship: Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Conant, Staying Roman (2012)
Courtois, Les Vandales et l'Afrique (1955)

set.detail: On 26 January 447 a series of severe earthquakes struck Constantinople and the surrounding region, throwing down large sections of the land walls, including 57 towers, while the people took refuge outside the city and processed barefoot with the emperor to the Hebdomon, chanting the Trisagion. The timing was disastrous: Attila was moving against the eastern empire with his largest army, and the plague had broken out. The praetorian prefect Flavius Constantinus organised the reconstruction, mobilising the members of the circus factions, the Blues and the Greens, as labour gangs, each responsible for a section. The work was completed, according to the inscriptions, in sixty days. The inscriptions on the Mevlevihane gate (the Rhegium gate) say in Greek that 'by the emperor's command Constantinus built this strong wall in sixty days', and in Latin that 'by the orders of Theodosius, Constantinus built these strong walls in less than two months; even Pallas could hardly have built so stout a citadel so quickly'. Constantinus also added the outer wall and the moat that made the Theodosian Walls a triple defence. Attila, who defeated the eastern field army at the Utus and raided to Thermopylae, did not attack the city. In the Peace of Anatolius later that year the East agreed to pay arrears of 6,000 lb of gold and an annual tribute of 2,100 lb, and to evacuate a strip of land south of the Danube five days' journey wide. The episode shows the importance of the walls to eastern survival and the organisation of urban manpower through the factions.

scholarship: Croke, 'The date and circumstances of Marcian's decree', Byzantion 48 (1978)
Crow, 'The infrastructures of a great city' (2007)

set.detail: In 449 Theodosius II sent the senior officer Maximinus as envoy to Attila, accompanied by his friend the historian Priscus of Panium, whose account is the most vivid description of the Hunnic court to survive. Unknown to Maximinus, the eunuch Chrysaphius had bribed Attila's envoy Edeco, with the interpreter Vigilas as go-between, to assassinate Attila. Edeco revealed the plot to his master. The embassy travelled through the ruins of Naissus, still strewn with bones after the sack of 442, crossed the Danube and followed Attila north to his residence on the Hungarian plain, a complex of wooden buildings and palisades, with a bath built of stone brought from Pannonia by a Roman captive architect. Priscus describes Attila's banquets, where he ate from a wooden plate while his guests had silver, the singers who celebrated his victories, a Moorish dwarf jester named Zercon, and Attila's wife Kreka. He records a famous conversation with a Greek merchant from Viminacium who had been captured, won his freedom fighting for the Huns, and now preferred life among them to the injustice, taxation and corrupt courts of the empire; Priscus answers with a defence of Roman law. Vigilas, returning with 50 lb of gold for the assassination, was seized, and Attila sent envoys to Constantinople with the moneybag hanging round Vigilas's neck, demanding Chrysaphius's head. Theodosius sent the patricians Anatolius and Nomus, who bought peace with gifts and secured the return of prisoners and land. The episode illustrates Roman diplomacy, the intelligence networks of the Hunnic court, and the presence of Romans in Hunnic service, among them Attila's secretary Orestes, the father of Romulus Augustulus.

scholarship: Blockley, The Fragmentary Classicising Historians of the Later Roman Empire II (1983)
Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)

set.detail: Theodosius II, emperor since 402 and sole eastern ruler since 408, died on 28 July 450 at the age of 49 after a fall from his horse while hunting near the Lycus river. His reign, the longest of any Roman emperor, had seen the building of the land walls, the Theodosian Code, the foundation of the school at the Capitol (425), the Councils of Ephesus (431 and 449), and the costly appeasement of Attila. He left no son: his daughter Licinia Eudoxia was married to Valentinian III, and the western emperor might have claimed the eastern throne. Instead power was settled by his sister Pulcheria, Augusta since 414 and a consecrated virgin, who had been eclipsed in the 440s by the eunuch Chrysaphius. With the support of the magister militum Aspar, she chose Marcian, a retired officer from Thrace who had served under Aspar, and married him on the condition that she keep her vow of virginity. Marcian was proclaimed on 25 August 450 at the Hebdomon, perhaps crowned by the patriarch Anatolius, although the role of the patriarch in coronations is debated for this date. The new regime reversed Theodosius's last policies at once: Chrysaphius was executed, tribute to Attila was stopped, and a new council was summoned that met at Chalcedon in 451 and overturned the Robber Synod. The western court did not recognise Marcian until 452. Theodosius was later remembered as a pious and learned but weak ruler, dominated by his sister, his wife Eudocia and his eunuchs, an image modern historians have partly revised to stress the effectiveness of his government.

scholarship: Holum, Theodosian Empresses (1982)
Millar, A Greek Roman Empire: Power and Belief under Theodosius II (2006)
Burgess, 'The accession of Marcian', BZ 86/87 (1993/4)

set.detail: In 451 Attila turned west, claiming that Valentinian's sister Honoria had offered herself to him in marriage and that half the western empire was her dowry; he may also have intended to attack the Visigoths. His army of Huns and subject peoples, Ostrogoths, Gepids, Rugi, Sciri, Heruli, Thuringians and others, crossed the Rhine, sacked Metz on 7 April and besieged Orléans, which the bishop Anianus held until Aetius arrived in June with a coalition of the Roman army, the Visigoths of Theodoric I, the Alans of Sangiban, Franks, Burgundians, Saxons, Armorican and other groups. Attila retreated to the Campus Mauriacus, apparently in Champagne between Troyes and Châlons. The battle, around 20 June 451, began with a struggle for a ridge, which the Romans and Visigoths won. In the main fighting Theodoric was killed, trampled by his own men or struck by an Ostrogothic javelin, and his son Thorismund led a charge that broke the Hunnic line. Attila retreated into his wagon laager and had a pyre built of saddles to burn himself if the camp were stormed. Jordanes, following Cassiodorus and probably Priscus, gives the impossible figure of 165,000 dead. Aetius did not press the siege; he persuaded Thorismund to return to Toulouse to secure his throne, perhaps to avoid strengthening the Goths too much. Attila withdrew across the Rhine and invaded Italy in 452. The battle has been called one of the decisive battles of world history, but modern scholars stress that Attila's power was not broken by it: it was rather an inconclusive defence that demonstrated Aetius's diplomacy and the dependence of the western empire on its federates.
set.debate: The site is unknown; candidates include Montgueux near Troyes and Châlons-en-Champagne. The date of 20 June is not certain.

scholarship: Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Kim, The Huns (2016)
Bury, History of the Later Roman Empire I (1923)

set.detail: The Second Council of Ephesus of 449, dominated by Dioscorus of Alexandria, had restored Eutyches, deposed Flavian of Constantinople, who died after rough treatment, and refused to read the Tome of Leo; Leo called it a latrocinium, a robbery. After Theodosius's death, Marcian and Pulcheria summoned a new council, first to Nicaea and then to Chalcedon, close enough for imperial control. It met in the church of St Euphemia from 8 October to 1 November 451, with some 500 bishops, nearly all eastern, under the presidency of imperial commissioners; papal legates attended. In the first session the acts of Ephesus II were read and Dioscorus was condemned, and in the third he was deposed for disobedience. The Tome of Leo was read and acclaimed with the cry 'Peter has spoken through Leo; Cyril taught thus'. Under imperial pressure the bishops agreed in the fifth session on a definition of faith confessing one and the same Christ 'in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation', the distinction of natures not being removed by the union, with each nature preserving its property and coming together in one person and one hypostasis. The council also passed canons, among them canon 28, which gave Constantinople privileges equal to Rome's as the New Rome and jurisdiction over the dioceses of Pontus, Asia and Thrace; Leo's legates protested and the pope refused to ratify it. Chalcedon, counted as the Fourth Ecumenical Council, became the touchstone of orthodoxy in Rome and Constantinople, but Egypt, much of Syria and Armenia rejected it as Nestorian. The resulting division into Chalcedonian and anti-Chalcedonian (Miaphysite) churches dominated imperial religious politics for two centuries, through the Henotikon, the Three Chapters and monoenergism.

scholarship: Price and Gaddis, The Acts of the Council of Chalcedon (2005)
Grillmeier, Christ in Christian Tradition II.1 (1987)
Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972)

set.detail: In spring 452 Attila, frustrated in Gaul, crossed the Julian Alps into Italy, which Aetius had left undefended. The first target was Aquileia, the great port and fortress at the head of the Adriatic, one of the largest cities of Italy with a mint and the seat of a bishop. The Huns besieged it for about three months. Jordanes and Procopius tell that Attila was about to abandon the siege when he saw storks carrying their young away from the city, interpreted it as an omen that the city was doomed, and ordered a final assault, which succeeded. Aquileia was destroyed so thoroughly, Jordanes says, that hardly a trace of it remained; this is an exaggeration, since the city continued as a bishopric, but it never recovered its earlier importance. Later Venetian legend made refugees from Aquileia and other mainland cities the founders of settlements in the lagoons, such as Grado and Torcello, where the patriarch of Aquileia later took refuge from the Lombards. After Aquileia the Huns took Concordia, Altinum, Patavium, Vicetia, Verona, Brixia, Bergamum, Mediolanum and Ticinum; at Milan, the Suda says, Attila saw a painting of Roman emperors with Scythians at their feet and had a painter show himself with the emperors pouring out gold at his feet. Famine and disease weakened his army, Marcian sent troops across the Danube to attack the Hunnic homeland, and an eastern army under another Aetius reached Italy. These factors, as much as the embassy of Pope Leo, explain Attila's withdrawal. The destruction of Aquileia marked the end of its role as the principal city of north-eastern Italy, a role inherited by Cividale and later Venice.

scholarship: Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)

set.detail: After the sack of the cities of the Po valley in summer 452, the western court sent an embassy to Attila, encamped near the Mincio close to Mantua: the former consul and prefect Gennadius Avienus, the former prefect Trygetius, an experienced negotiator who had made the treaty of 435 with the Vandals, and Pope Leo I. The embassy secured Attila's withdrawal from Italy. Prosper, a member of Leo's household, gives the credit to the pope: Attila received the envoys and was so pleased by the presence of the high priest that he promised peace and withdrew beyond the Danube. Jordanes, following Priscus, adds that Attila's advisers warned him of the fate of Alaric, who had died soon after taking Rome. Later hagiography, embodied in Raphael's fresco in the Vatican, has the apostles Peter and Paul appear in the sky with swords threatening Attila. Hydatius, a contemporary in Spain, gives a different account: famine and plague were destroying the Huns, and auxiliaries sent by Marcian under a general named Aetius had attacked them in Italy and their homeland, forcing withdrawal. Modern historians combine the factors: the Hunnic army, unable to besiege Rome after a long campaign, was suffering from disease and lack of supplies in a land that had suffered famine in 451, and the eastern counter-offensive threatened its base, so the embassy offered a face-saving agreement, probably with payments. The episode became central to papal prestige: Leo's intervention, with his reported negotiation with Gaiseric in 455, established the bishop of Rome as the city's defender, a role later claimed by Gregory the Great.

scholarship: Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Wessel, Leo the Great and the Spiritual Rebuilding of a Universal Rome (2008)

set.detail: Attila died in early 453, probably in his residence in the Hungarian plain, after a feast celebrating his marriage to a young woman named Ildico, one of many wives. Jordanes, quoting Priscus, says that he drank heavily, lay down on his back, and suffered a haemorrhage from the nose that choked him in his sleep; in the morning his attendants broke down the door and found him dead and the bride weeping beneath her veil. Marcellinus Comes, writing in the sixth century, records a rumour that Ildico stabbed him; the later Germanic legend of Kriemhild or Gudrun avenging her kin on Atli developed from this. The funeral described by Jordanes followed steppe custom: horsemen rode around his body lying in state in a silk tent, singing a funeral song which Jordanes paraphrases; the warriors cut their hair and slashed their faces so that the greatest of warriors should be mourned not with women's tears but with men's blood. He was buried at night in three coffins of gold, silver and iron, with weapons and treasure, and the workers who dug the grave were killed so that it would never be found. Priscus also reports that Marcian dreamed on the same night of a broken bow. Attila's death led quickly to the break-up of his empire. His sons Ellac, Dengizich and Ernak quarrelled over the inheritance, and the subject peoples led by Ardaric of the Gepids rebelled and defeated them at the Nedao in 454. Within twenty years the Hunnic empire had disappeared, and the peoples it had ruled, Ostrogoths, Gepids, Rugi, Sciri and Heruli, became the new powers of the Danube and Italy.

scholarship: Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)
Kim, The Huns (2016)

set.detail: After Attila's death, his sons, whom Jordanes describes as dividing the peoples among themselves like household slaves, fought over the succession. Ardaric, king of the Gepids and one of Attila's most trusted subordinates, led a revolt of the subject peoples. The decisive battle was fought in 454 at the river Nedao in Pannonia, whose location is unknown. Jordanes describes a remarkable spectacle: Goths fighting with pikes, Gepids with swords, Rugi breaking spears in their wounds, Suebi on foot, Huns with bows, Alans with heavy armour, Heruli with light weapons. The Gepids and their allies won; Attila's eldest son Ellac was killed with some 30,000 Huns and their allies. The battle broke Hunnic power in central Europe. The Gepids took over the Hungarian plain east of the Danube and Dacia, with their centre at Sirmium in the sixth century. The Ostrogoths, whose participation in the battle is unclear, received land as federates in Pannonia from Marcian, under the brothers Valamir, Thiudimir and Vidimir. Other groups, Sciri, Rugi, Heruli and Alans, were settled in the Danube provinces or moved into Roman service. The surviving Huns under Dengizich and Ernak retreated east towards the Black Sea steppe, where Dengizich was killed in 469. The Nedao thus marks the transition from the Hunnic empire to the successor kingdoms of the Danube, from which Theodoric's Ostrogoths and Odoacer's following would emerge to rule Italy. The Gepids, as the winners, remained a significant power until they were destroyed by the Lombards and Avars in 567. Jordanes, himself of Gothic-Alan descent, is the only narrative source.
set.debate: Location (perhaps a tributary of the Sava in Pannonia) and exact date (454 or 455) are uncertain; the Ostrogoths may have fought on either side.

scholarship: Heather, Empires and Barbarians (2009)
Kim, The Huns (2016)
Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)

set.detail: Flavius Aetius had dominated the western empire for twenty years, as magister militum and patricius, holding three consulships (432, 437, 446) and defending Gaul with Hunnic and federate troops. By 454 his position seemed secure: he had persuaded Valentinian III to betroth his younger daughter Placidia to Aetius's son Gaudentius, linking the general's family to the dynasty. This alarmed the court, especially the senator Petronius Maximus and the eunuch primicerius sacri cubiculi Heraclius, who persuaded Valentinian that Aetius intended to kill him. On 21 or 22 September 454, during a meeting in the palace at Rome to discuss finances, Valentinian, aged 35, accused Aetius of treason, drew his sword, and with Heraclius cut him down. The praetorian prefect Boethius, a friend of Aetius, was killed at the same time. Sidonius Apollinaris, Prosper and Procopius tell the story with variations; Procopius has a courtier tell Valentinian afterwards that he had cut off his right hand with his left. The murder deprived the West of its most capable general and its links to the federate peoples. It brought about Valentinian's own death six months later, when two of Aetius's bucellarii, Optila and Thraustila, killed him on the Campus Martius at Petronius Maximus's instigation. With the end of the Theodosian dynasty in 455 the western empire entered its final phase of short-lived emperors controlled by generals such as Ricimer. The Vandals, whose treaty of 442 depended on the betrothal of Huneric to Eudocia, felt released from their obligations and sacked Rome in 455.

scholarship: Stickler, Aëtius (2002)
Hughes, Aetius: Attila's Nemesis (2012)

set.detail: Petronius Maximus, a senator of great wealth who had held two consulships and the urban and praetorian prefectures, had helped persuade Valentinian III to murder Aetius in 454. Disappointed of the position of patricius that he hoped to inherit, Maximus approached two of Aetius's former bodyguards, the Huns or Goths Optila and Thraustila, now in the emperor's guard, and encouraged them to avenge their master. On 16 March 455, as Valentinian rode to the Campus Martius to watch athletic exercises near the Two Laurels, Optila struck him on the temple and Thraustila killed the eunuch Heraclius; the emperor's guards did not intervene, and the killers took the imperial diadem and robe to Maximus. The assassination ended the Theodosian dynasty in the West after 76 years. Valentinian was 35 and left two daughters, Eudocia, betrothed to Huneric, and Placidia, married to the senator Olybrius. The next day, the army and Senate proclaimed Petronius Maximus emperor. He forced Valentinian's widow Licinia Eudoxia to marry him and married his son Palladius to Eudocia, breaking the Vandal engagement. Procopius says that Eudoxia, outraged, appealed to Gaiseric for help. Whether or not this is true, Gaiseric seized the pretext and his fleet appeared at Portus at the end of May 455. Maximus, who had reigned less than three months, fled and was killed by the crowd or by soldiers on 31 May. The assassination of Valentinian and the Vandal sack together mark the beginning of the end for the western empire: the following twenty-one years saw nine emperors, mostly puppets of generals, and the shrinking of the western state to Italy.

scholarship: Mathisen, 'Petronius Maximus', De Imperatoribus Romanis (online)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)

set.detail: Gaiseric's fleet landed at Portus at the end of May 455, using as a pretext the breaking of the engagement between his son Huneric and Valentinian's daughter Eudocia, and perhaps responding to an appeal from Licinia Eudoxia. The emperor Petronius Maximus panicked and fled, and was killed on 31 May by a mob or by imperial servants who stoned him or tore him apart. On 2 June the Vandals entered Rome without resistance. According to Prosper, Pope Leo I met Gaiseric outside the gates and persuaded him to refrain from burning, torture and murder; the account may be an embellishment parallel to Leo's meeting with Attila. The sack lasted fourteen days, much longer than Alaric's three days in 410, and was systematic. The Vandals removed the treasures of the imperial palace, half the gilded bronze roof tiles of the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, statues, and, according to Procopius, the treasures of the Temple of Jerusalem brought to Rome by Titus, which Belisarius later recovered at Carthage and Justinian returned to Jerusalem. They took thousands of captives to Africa, among them Licinia Eudoxia and her daughters Eudocia and Placidia; Eudocia married Huneric and became mother of Hilderic. Bishop Deogratias of Carthage sold church plate to ransom captives and housed them in two basilicas. The term vandalism, coined by the Abbé Grégoire in 1794, has unfairly fixed the Vandals' reputation: the sack was a plunder for wealth, not a wanton destruction. Politically, it destroyed what remained of western prestige, gave Gaiseric hostages from the imperial family, and led to the Visigothic-backed proclamation of Avitus in Gaul in July 455.

scholarship: Merrills and Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Steinacher, Die Vandalen (2016)
